content: Task shifting can influence interprofessional relationships and collaborative practices. Multidisciplinary training opportunities can foster mutual respect and trust among healthcare providers. Establishing formal systems for interprofessional communication, such as regular meeting schedules, can enhance collaboration and help resolve conflicts effectively. When task shifting involves reorganizing patient flow processes, it often leads to an increase in referrals across different levels of healthcare services. Systems must be implemented to manage and adapt to these changes. Referral systems function more efficiently when there are strong relationships between healthcare cadres and a clear understanding of the roles of different providers. Conversely, distrust among providers can hinder timely referrals. Patients generally express confidence in the competence of less highly trained healthcare providers. However, in certain settings or for specific tasks, patients may prefer care from providers with higher levels of training. Patient satisfaction with task shifting is influenced by how well the programs address their needs, the extent to which they are consulted during program development, and their access to alternative care options. Task shifting to less trained cadres can reduce barriers between patients and providers, such as those related to language, social status, gender, and physical accessibility. However, when tasks related to stigmatized conditions are shifted to providers from the same community, concerns about confidentiality and privacy may arise. Pre-service and in-service training for healthcare workers often face challenges, including insufficient training opportunities, training that does not align with practical needs, unqualified trainers, rigid schedules, and unrealistic requirements. Beyond clinical supervision, healthcare workers require emotional support and guidance on liability issues. Challenges in supervision include inadequate supervision, unprepared or unconfident supervisors, time constraints, logistical issues (e.g., lack of funds for travel to peripheral facilities), and bureaucratic hurdles. Field-based supervision, closely tied to daily working conditions and peer interaction, can improve provider support. Using evidence-informed global guidance, such as WHO recommendations, can help countries enhance their health system performance. However, developing or modifying health policies and systems is a complex process. Most guidance documents do not contextualize recommendations to specific national needs, particularly regarding health and political systems. The Optimize MNH guidance offers an eight-step framework for contextualizing health systems guidance at the national level. This process includes clarifying the problem, framing options, identifying implementation considerations, and considering the broader health and political system contexts. Monitoring and evaluation are essential to determine whether policies are implemented as expected and whether they achieve desired outcomes. The dissemination and implementation of evidence-based policies related to task shifting require well-planned, participatory, and consensus-driven processes. The WHO has adopted a formal Knowledge-to-Action framework to guide the dissemination, adaptation, and implementation of its recommendations. These recommendations will be shared through a network of international partners, including WHO offices, Ministries of Health, collaborating centers, UN agencies, and NGOs. Policy briefs and other materials will be developed to engage policymakers, program managers, and clinicians. Successful implementation depends on adapting recommendations to the local context and ensuring participatory processes. Future research on task shifting should address the paucity of reliable data, particularly regarding mid-level providers such as auxiliary nurses and associate clinicians. Qualitative research alongside trials of task-shifting interventions can provide insights into the reasons behind trial outcomes. Research should also explore the roles and effectiveness of different health worker configurations, the cost-effectiveness of interventions, and the factors influencing provider-patient relationships and community acceptance.
